Harvest quadrature can change a discrete optimal control problem even when the state scheme stays fixed. We study this effect for a positivity-preserving Lotka– Volterra scheme. The difference appears in a model with harvesting alone: rewarding the scheme’s removal flux gives a strictly convex reduced cost, whereas using prey density at the start of each step overestimates harvest and can create negative curvature and a strict local minimum that is not global. Rational root isolation certifies the two-step global minimizers. With diffusion in one space dimension, nonnegative bounded H1 initial data and positive diffusivities, the costs, weighted gradients and Hessians differ by O(τ ) uniformly in the spatial mesh, where τ is the time step. A uniform positive lower bound on the reduced Hessian gives the same order for the distance between nearby controls. A large enough effort penalty gives unique global discrete minimizers. We also prove positivity, exact population balance and a common variational limit, and derive exact discrete adjoints and Hessian actions. Numerical tests trace changes in curvature and stationary controls across parameters and grids, with costs evaluated on a common reference using adaptive time stepping. The construction extends to weighted production–destruction systems, giving exact harvest accounting and smooth derivatives on fixed grids.
Keywords: reaction–diffusion, optimal harvesting, positive scheme, exact discrete adjoint, reduced Hessian, variational convergence, forward–backward sweep.

Harvesting removes prey and leaves less food for predators, while dif fusion spreads both effects in space [2, 3, 4, 5, 37]. At position x and time t, we write v1 (x, t) and v2(x, t) for predator and prey densities, and u(x, t) for fishing effort. The objective balances population tracking, effort costs and harvest reward. Discretizing this problem means choosing how to approximate both the dynamics and the reward [32, 31, 29, 34, 30].

Implicit–explicit (IMEX) Euler treats diffusion implicitly and reactions explicitly, preserving nonnegativity under a time-step restriction [6, 7] . A Patankar production– destruction step preserves positivity for every time step [8]. How, then, should harvest be counted over a step? To separate the effects of the state scheme and the reward, we compare three discrete problems. I uses IMEX and the prey density at the start of the step. P0 and P1 share the same triangular positive scheme but use prey density at the start and end of the step, respectively. These are the old-state and new-state rules. Comparing I with P0 isolates the state scheme, and comparing P0 with P1 isolates harvest quadrature.

The new-state rule rewards exactly the removal flux in the population balance. In the model with harvesting alone, the old-state rule overestimates removal. That extra reward can create negative curvature in directions that redistribute effort between time steps, add a strict local minimum, and favor extreme allocations at fixed total effort. For the full discrete problem, we derive state bounds uniform in the control and mesh, exact discrete adjoints, and Hessian-vector products that require no assembled Hessian matrix [10, 11]. Because the reward depends on the final prey state, its derivative enters the terminal adjoint condition.

For the positive scheme with diffusion in one dimension, we bound the gradient and Hessian differences uniformly in the mesh. Under coercivity, these bounds control the change in the optimal control. On Ω = (0, 1), with nonnegative bounded H1 initial data, all three problems have the same weak-∗ variational limit. Discrete controls whose costs approach the discrete global minimum have subsequences converging strongly in L 2 to continuous global minimizers, and discrete local minimizers approximate every strict L 2 local minimizer.

The numerical tests check the derivatives and compare four optimizers on a common reference. Parameter continuation and grid refinement then trace the effects of quadrature on temporal switching, sensitivity to the initial control and reduced curvature. For relaxed forward– backward sweep (FBS), we give an exact local contraction criterion: under strict complementarity and a positive definite Hessian on the free coordinates, the criterion depends on that Hessian’s smallest and largest eigenvalues.

This analysis builds on consistent discrete adjoints and second derivatives [12, 13, 14, 15], together with the positivity, conservation and accuracy of Patankar schemes [8, 16, 9]. Cacace et al. study production–destruction control by dynamic programming with a modified Patankar semi-Lagrangian scheme [17]. Here we examine how harvest quadrature changes curvature, derivatives and controls.
